hpi_details: 60F presents with a 2-day history of a rapidly spreading red, warm, and swollen area on her left lower leg. It is very painful to touch. She also has a fever of 38.5C and chills. She had a minor scratch on her shin a few days ago.
concerns: worried she might lose her leg

core_concepts: Infection of the deep dermis and subcutaneous tissue, most commonly caused by Beta-hemolytic streptococci or S. aureus.
common_misconceptions: Confusing bilateral stasis dermatitis with bilateral cellulitis (true cellulitis is almost always unilateral).
dangerous_errors: Missing necrotizing fasciitis (pain out of proportion, crepitus, hemorrhagic bullae, rapid progression).
management_principles: Oral or IV antibiotics targeting Strep and Staph. Leg elevation.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

source_refs.title: Infectious Diseases Society of America (IDSA) Clinical Practice Guidelines

reference_soap.subjective: 60F with rapidly spreading, painful, unilateral leg erythema and fever after minor trauma.
reference_soap.objective: T 38.5C. Left lower leg has a large, ill-defined, blanching erythematous plaque that is warm and tender. No crepitus or fluctuance.
reference_soap.assessment: Uncomplicated cellulitis of left lower extremity.
reference_soap.plan: Start an oral agent active against streptococci for nonpurulent cellulitis, such as cephalexin when appropriate. If MRSA coverage is needed, use an agent with reliable streptococcal coverage or combine therapy as appropriate; trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole alone has unreliable streptococcal activity. Mark margins, elevate the leg, and reassess within 48 hours or sooner for systemic deterioration.

learning_objectives: Recognize typical features of cellulitis and rule out necrotizing fasciitis.

teaching.one_liner: Unilateral, poorly demarcated erythema, warmth, and swelling of the lower leg with fever.

must_ask.say: When did the redness start, and has it been spreading?
Did you have any cut, scratch, or injury to that leg recently?
Have you had a fever or chills?
On a scale of 1 to 10, how bad is the pain, and does it seem worse than the redness would suggest?
Have you noticed any blistering, dark discoloration, or a crackling feeling under the skin?

history.answer: My left lower leg has turned bright red, swollen, and it hurts terribly to touch.
It began about two days ago as a small reddish spot on my left shin, and it has spread quickly across my calf.
The redness and swelling are only on my left lower leg; my right leg looks completely normal.
The skin looks bright red, shiny, and swollen, but there are no blisters, crusts, or open draining sores.
It throbs, burns, and hurts a lot when touched, but the pain matches where it looks inflamed and it isn't numb.
No, it hasn't faded or come and gone at all; it has just expanded continuously.
I bumped and got a small scratch on my left shin while moving a box a few days ago.
Yes, I started having shaking chills yesterday evening and my fever spiked to 38.5 degrees Celsius.
No, the skin is still intact with no peeling, purple spots, or black dead tissue.
No, there are no fluid blisters, pus pockets, or fluid leaking from the skin.
No, my mouth, eyes, and private areas have no sores, redness, or ulcers.
No facial or lip swelling, no throat tightness, and no shortness of breath.
I wondered if a spider bit me while I was cleaning out the basement, though I didn't see one bite me.
No recent hiking, no travel, and I haven't been in any swimming pools, public baths, or hot tubs.
No, I haven't used any new body soaps, lotions, detergents, or tried unfamiliar foods.
No, my husband is completely healthy and has no skin problems or rash.
I've never had a leg infection or anything like this happen before.
I rubbed a tiny bit of petroleum jelly on the initial scratch, but I haven't put any prescription cream or ointment on it.
My knee and ankle joints move normally and don't hurt inside; it is just the skin and tissue of my calf that hurt.
No, my toenails look normal and I have no rashes on my scalp or between my toes.
No, I have never had eczema, asthma, or seasonal allergies.
I have been married to my husband for over thirty years, and I have no genital ulcers or discharge.
I really think a poisonous spider or some insect must have bitten my shin in the basement.
I am terrified that this is spreading so fast I might end up losing my leg.
I am hoping you can prescribe strong antibiotics to get rid of this infection.
I have type 2 diabetes and my doctor told me I have mild fluid swelling in both my lower legs.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been hospitalized.
I take metformin for my blood sugar and amlodipine for my blood pressure every morning.
I have no known allergies to penicillin or any other medications.
I have never smoked in my life, and I only have an occasional glass of wine maybe once a month.
I am retired and spend most of my time at home reading or watching television.
My mother had high blood pressure and diabetes, but no one in my family has had blood clots or chronic skin problems.
I went through menopause naturally about nine years ago, when I was fifty-one.

exam.finding: Temperature 38.5°C, blood pressure 134/82 mmHg, heart rate 94 beats per minute, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
Alert and oriented, appears mildly uncomfortable and flushed, resting in bed with left leg extended.
Large, ill-defined, blanching erythematous plaque across the left lower leg that is noticeably warm and tender; no fluctuance, bullae, skin necrosis, or crepitus.
Left calf is swollen, warm, and diffusely tender to palpation; right calf is soft, non-tender, and without swelling or acute erythema.
Mild 1+ pitting edema on the right lower extremity, and 2+ pitting edema on the swollen left lower leg.
Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are 2+ and symmetric bilaterally; capillary refill is under 2 seconds in all toes.
A tender, enlarged left inguinal lymph node is palpable at approximately 1.5 cm; no inguinal hernia identified.
Oral mucosa is pink, moist, and intact without ulcers, vesicles, or mucosal lesions.
Conjunctivae are normal without pallor, petechiae, or conjunctival injection; sclerae are non-icteric.
